newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's 2nd ENI sale seen as good strategy.
newsitem.headline: Italy's 2nd ENI sale seen as good strategy.

text.p: The Italian Treasury's move to sell just 10 percent in the second phase privatisation of energy giant ENI is below market expectations but analysts said on Monday the drip-feed strategy was a winner.
The Italian Treasury said on Sunday it was offering a total of 700 million ordinary shares in the second tranche of the sale of ENI, the country's largest publicly traded company.

Giving further details on Monday, the Treasury said Italian retail investors would be offered 300 million shares, there will be an institutional offering of 235 million shares and an offering of 165 million shares in the United States.

Global coordinators for the sale, Italian IMI bank and CS First Boston have also been granted an over-allotment, or "green shoe" option of 105 million shares to meet possible over demand by institutional investors.

Treasury director Mario Draghi told a news conference on Monday that the ENI offer, of 8.75 percent of share capital but nearly 10 percent of the group including the green shoe amount, could be increased if demand was strong enough.
The total offer is valued at some six trillion lire ($4 billion). Draghi said the second tranche sale was likely to be the largest European share offer so far this year.
For the first time in Italy shares will be offered to Italian retail investors at a discount. Also, those who hold their shares for a year will get one bonus share for every 10 bought.
Last November, the Treasury sold a first 15 percent tranche of ENI, which has a market capitalisation of some $35 billion.

It was floated at 5,250 lire to trade in Milan, London and New York and brought 6.3 trillion lire into the state coffers. ENI shares traded 2.99 percent up at 7,520 lire in Milan at 1300 GMT. The stock hit a year's high of 7,925 lire on July 2.
"Some in the market had been expecting a 15 to 20 percent sale, but those in the know saw 10 percent as realistic," said one London equity analyst who declined to be named.

He said the Treasury, which will hold about 76 percent of ENI shares following the offering, would be making further offerings but still had to oversee the privatisation of state telecoms group Stet and electricity utility ENEL, both set for early next year.
"It is still a considerable chunk," he said. "The shares are appealing and the share price will likely rise above current levels."
Marco Nascimbeni, head of operations at Milan securities house Carnegie Italia Sim, said the 10 percent sale was less than many expected but that the Treasury strategy was well thought out.

"ENI shares are outperforming the market on worries there wont be enough shares to go around. Given the current lack of liquidity on the stock market, the Treasury did not want to depress the stock price by offering, say 20 percent. This is a good strategy and they could well up the offer. The final figure will depend on private investor demand," he said.
He said market expectations were for a share offer price of between 7,200 to 7,300 lire putting a value of about 5.8 trillion lire on the placement.
"The Treasury won't be too demanding in terms of price. Their aim is to keep ENI shareholders happy.
"ENI's privatisation will be step by step and we can look forward to another couple of tasty placings before the Treasury gets its stake down to 51 percent," Nascimbeni added.
The Treasury, which will retain control of ENI, has not indicated its plans for further sell-offs of the energy group.

A series of world-wide road shows start on Monday in Milan and the Italian public sale runs from October 21 to 25. The share price will be fixed on October 26 and trading is expected to start on October 28. $=1,515 lire
